claims.text: The combined printing, hydrogen de-binding, getter-assisted vacuum sintering, water quenching, and silicide coating treatment will overcome the poor oxygen resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without compromising its high-temperature mechanical properties.
The initial ink is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr blend made from HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5, TiH2, ZrH2, and metallic Ti/Nb in a polystyrene/binder matrix.
Vacuum sintering at 1400 °C for 18 hours at below 3×10^-6 torr with a titanium-sponge getter will produce the desired alloy state.
Water quenching from 1500 °C will retain a metastable beta-BCC phase.
A silicide coating will provide self-healing oxidation protection.
The hydrides decompose sequentially in the order Ta, Nb, then Hf/Ti/Zr.
Sequential hydride decomposition enables in-situ alloying and oxygen scavenging.
The treatment will result in approximately 1.0 wt.% oxygen uptake.
The processed alloy will form a metastable single beta-BCC phase.
The titanium-sponge getter scavenges oxygen during sintering.
Approximately 1.0 wt.% interstitial oxygen will strengthen the alloy without forming brittle embrittling phases.
Rapid water quenching suppresses formation of brittle alpha-HCP structure.
The silicide coating forms self-healing (Zr,Hf)O2 layers that significantly slow further oxidation.
The treatment will produce a nearly fully dense bulk material.
The treated material will retain useful tensile ductility and yield strength, including at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
The treated material will have a significantly lower oxidation rate than cast or uncoated sintered HfNbTaTiZr.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr suffers from rapid oxidation, cracking, and alpha-HCP embrittlement.
An 18-hour sintering duration is sufficient for full densification.
Slower quenching or insufficient oxygen scavenging will likely produce a mixed-phase microstructure and poorer oxidation resistance.
